title: The Queue Outside

post.author: u/brindle_lane_door
post.title: I work the door at a club. Since June, one ticket has come back to the top of the box every 1.5 seconds. Last night a second one joined it.

blocks.text: I work the door at the Mothlight, a club in two railway arches on Brindle Lane. We open at 22:00, and a guest arrives about every 10 seconds. They scan a code by the door and type a name and an email address. The club's web server, the computer that answers their phones, signs them up. Nobody gets in until their phone says *You're on the list*. The welcome email carries the code that gets them back in after a smoke. Fenna, who built the app, says saving a signup takes 0.1 seconds. The email provider, a company that sends emails for us, takes 1.5 seconds to send one. And the server works on 8 signups at once, each on its own thread, one of its 8 pairs of hands.

Until May, each signup went in three steps while the guest's phone waited: save it, send the email, then answer. Every Saturday at 23:00 the late train empties onto Brindle Lane, and about 600 people sign up in a minute, 10 a second. The server could finish only 5 a second. Phones spun for up to a minute and the line froze on the pavement. It was like walking every guest to the cloakroom myself.

In May Fenna changed it. Now the server takes three quick steps. It saves the signup. It drops a ticket, a note that says *send this guest's email*, in what she calls the box. Then it answers at once with the ticket number, which is also the guest's hook in Clodagh's cloakroom. Two workers, small programs that do nothing else, send the emails. Each takes the ticket on top of the box, sends its email, then takes the next. If a send fails, the ticket goes back on top and is tried again. The line hasn't stopped since.

On Saturday 13 June, guest 413 typed *back for my coat* where his email address should go. He never came back. Worker-1 has tried his email every 1.5 seconds since that night, about 6.9 million times, Fenna says. Every Saturday since, the late train's emails have come up to 14 minutes late. His green wool coat is still on hook 413. Clodagh has taken it to lost property three times. Every Saturday it's back on the hook.

Last night at 02:00, ticket 2035 signed up with a comma where the dot goes. Fenna's log is the record the system writes as it works. Each line shows the time, then a ticket being saved and answered with 202, the server's code for *got it, not done yet*, or a worker failing a ticket, or how many tickets wait in the box and how many seconds the oldest has waited:

02:00:00.1  #2035  saved. answered 202. worker-2 takes it
02:00:01.6  worker-2  #2035 failed: not an email address. back on top
02:00:03.1  worker-2  #2035 failed: not an email address. back on top
02:30:00.0  box: 179 waiting, oldest 1,790 s
03:00:00.0  door shut. box: 359 waiting, oldest 3,590 s
05:00:00.0  box: 359 waiting, oldest 10,790 s
Nothing has left the box since 02:00. At 02:30 a man came back to the door with his phone held up. It still said *Welcome email: on its way*.
What should Fenna change before next Saturday?

blocks.label: fenna_dashboard_sat_0300.png

diagram.aria: Fenna's dashboard at 03:00:00 on Saturday. The door has shut. The web server still answers each signup with 202 in 0.1 seconds and has handed out 2,394 tickets tonight. The box, a queue, holds 359 tickets, the oldest waiting 3,590 seconds. Both workers are stuck: they send tickets 413 and 2035 to the email provider, which rejects them, and put them back on top. Nothing has been sent since 02:00.

blocks.caption: Fenna's dashboard at 03:00:00, redrawn. The web server still answers every signup with a 202 in 0.1 seconds, so the door never stopped. But both workers are retrying tickets that can't be sent: worker-1 has been on 413 since June, and worker-2 has been on 2035 since 02:00:00.1. Each failed ticket goes back on top and the same worker takes it again at once. Nothing has been sent since 02:00, and the box holds 359 tickets, the oldest waiting 3,590 seconds.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Some words first, then questions. A request is one message from a phone asking the server to do something. Work done while the guest waits for the answer is called synchronous: before May, the email was sent inside the request. Work done after the answer is called asynchronous, or background work. A queue is a waiting line for work: things go in at the back and come out at the front, in turn. Fenna's box is a queue, each ticket on it is a job, one piece of work, and the workers take jobs off and do them. And 202 Accepted is the status code, the three-digit number at the start of every answer, for what the server says now: I have your request, and it isn't finished. Now the evidence. Before May, 8 signups at once at 1.6 seconds each: how many a second, against the 10 the late train brings? Since June, how many workers have really been sending? Since 02:00, how many? Why did the door keep moving all night while nothing left the box? And what in Fenna's code ever decides that a ticket won't be tried again?

replies.author: u/brindle_lane_door
replies.text: Fenna did the sums: 5 a second against 10, so before May the line grew by 5 a second for the whole minute. Since June it's been one worker, about 0.7 a second, and since 02:00, none. On festival nights we get a guest a second all night, and she's glad last night wasn't one. Your last question she answered straight away. Nothing does.

comments.author: u/returned_mail_dorota
comments.text: Post offices had a name for letters they could neither deliver nor send back: dead letters, opened in a dead letter office to find out where they belonged. This board should find that familiar. Queues borrowed it. Queue people call each job a message. A dead-letter queue, or DLQ, is a second queue for messages that keep failing. It works in steps. A worker takes a message and fails. The queue counts that failure. Below the limit, the message goes back to be tried again. At the limit, it goes to the DLQ instead of back on top, and waits there for a person. Amazon SQS, short for Simple Queue Service, is a queue that Amazon runs for you. There the limit is maxReceiveCount, how many times a message can be handed out, set in the queue's redrive policy, its dead-letter settings. RabbitMQ is a program you run yourself to hold queues. Its quorum queues, a kind that keeps copies on several servers, have a delivery limit, 20 by default since version 4.0. But since 4.3, a message a worker hands back with nack, its way of saying *couldn't do it, put it back*, doesn't count. Two catches. A DLQ is a place to look, not a fix: set an alarm on it, a rule that calls someone when it fills, and make sure someone reads it. And don't set the limit so low that a provider's bad minute fills it with tickets that would have gone through on the next try.

comments.author: u/backoff_briony
comments.text: Fenna's loop has a name in RabbitMQ's docs. A consumer is another word for a worker. When a consumer puts a message back, it is requeued: returned to its old place if it can be, so at or near the head, the front of the queue. If the consumers keep putting it back, they make a requeue/redelivery loop: take it, fail, put it back, take it again. A message that can never succeed, like an address that isn't one, is a poison message. Retrying, trying again, is right for failures that pass, like a 503, the too-busy code, from a provider having a bad night. Then wait a little longer after each failed try, which is called backoff, and add jitter, a small random extra wait, so the retries don't all land at once. Retrying is wrong for failures that can't pass. And mind the other direction: SQS delivers at least once, sometimes more. A copy happens like this. A worker takes the ticket and sends the email. It dies before it tells SQS to delete the ticket. So the ticket comes back, and another worker sends it again. So make the job idempotent, safe to repeat: before sending, check whether this ticket's email already went.

replies.author: u/brindle_lane_door
replies.text: Fenna says the provider had a bad night in August: one email in five failed the first time with a 503 and went through on the second. She hadn't thought about a guest getting the same email twice. Clodagh says that would be the least strange thing about this place.

comments.author: u/oldest_ticket_augustin
comments.text: Watch the age, not just the count. 359 tickets in a box could be a busy night. A ticket that has waited an hour is an outage, a time the system isn't doing its job. SQS reports both numbers to CloudWatch, Amazon's service that records numbers about your systems over time. Each such number is called a metric. ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible is how many are waiting. ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage is how long the oldest has waited. An alarm on it works in steps: CloudWatch keeps checking the number; once it crosses the line you set, it sends someone a message. One odd detail. SQS leaves poison-pill messages, poison messages that are handed out again and again and never deleted, out of that age metric. So it wouldn't have shown you 413 itself, only the tickets piling up behind it. By my sums, an alarm at 10 minutes on the oldest ticket's age would have rung at about 23:11 every Saturday since June.

reply.prompt: Next Saturday the late train comes in at 23:00 as always. What should Fenna change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Go back to sending the email before answering, as before May, so a guest with a bad address finds out at the door.
options.part2: Fenna switched it back on Wednesday. On Saturday the late train came in at 23:00, and by 23:00:00.7 all 8 threads were busy. The server finished 5 signups a second against 10 arriving. At 23:01 there were 296 guests on the pavement waiting for a thread. The p95 wait, the time that 95 of every 100 guests waited within, was 30.4 seconds. The slowest phone spun for 61.6 seconds, and the line didn't clear until 23:02:00.6. At 02:00 a guest typed a comma where the dot goes, and 3.1 seconds later his phone told him the email had failed. He fixed it at the door. That part worked. When we closed, the green wool coat was still on hook 413.
options.senior: Sending the email inside the request ties every signup to the slowest step: 8 threads at 1.6 seconds each is 5 a second, and the late train brings 10. The one thing it did better was telling a guest about a bad address while he's still at the door. That doesn't need the email: check the address at signup, before the 202. The 2 AM problem was the retry rule, the rule for trying again, not the queue.

options.text: Run six workers instead of two, so even with a stuck ticket or two, the box empties within minutes of the rush.
options.part2: Fenna ran six workers on Saturday. Worker-1 was still on 413, but the other five took the late train's tickets: 399 in the box at 23:01, the last email sent at 23:03:00.5, two minutes after its guest signed up, and the box empty at 23:03:03.3. At 02:00 ticket 2035 came in with its comma, and a second worker started looping on it. By 03:00 the box was empty, and the two stuck workers had failed 12,005 times between them since just before 23:00. Fenna was pleased. I wasn't: two of six workers gone, and nothing to say so but a counter nobody watches. At 02:30 the man from ticket 2035 was at the door asking for his email, and when we closed his jacket was still on hook 2035, next to the green coat.
options.senior: More workers empty the box faster, and that clears the rush sooner. But retrying forever means every poison ticket, one that can never be sent, takes a worker for good: one since June, a second at 02:00, and the next bad address takes a third. Adding workers doesn't fix a loop. Cap the tries, park the failures where someone will look, and then choose how many workers the rush needs.

options.text: Give each ticket 3 tries, then throw it away, so a bad address can never hold a worker for more than 4.5 seconds.
options.part2: Fenna made the change on Wednesday. On Saturday at 22:59:51.5 ticket 413 failed its 6,854,401st try and was thrown away, and both workers went to the late train's tickets. The last one was sent at 23:07:30.2, and the box was empty at 23:08:01.6. At 02:00:04.6 ticket 2035 failed its third try and was thrown away too. Nothing on Fenna's dashboard changed colour. At 02:30 he was at the door with his phone, which still said *Welcome email: on its way*. Fenna searched for his ticket and couldn't find it anywhere: the box was empty, and there was nowhere else a ticket could be. When we closed there was a second coat nobody came back for, on hook 2035.
options.senior: Capping the tries frees the workers, and that's the right half. Throwing the ticket away is the wrong half: the guest never gets the email, and nobody can tell it happened or why. A dead-letter queue keeps the failed ticket where a person can read it, fix the cause and send it again, and an alarm on it says when to look.

options.text: Give each ticket 3 tries, then park it in a dead-letter queue; alarm on that queue and the oldest ticket's age.
options.part2: Fenna made the change on Wednesday, with one alarm for when the dead-letter queue holds anything and another for when the oldest ticket has waited 10 minutes. On Saturday at 22:59:51.5 ticket 413 failed its 6,854,401st try and went to the dead-letter queue, and her phone buzzed. Both workers took the late train: 519 tickets waiting at 23:01, the last email sent at 23:07:30.2 and the box empty at 23:08:01.6. The oldest ticket's age never passed 390 seconds, so the age alarm stayed quiet. At 02:00:04.6 ticket 2035 failed its third try and was parked, and her phone buzzed again. She read the address, put the dot back and sent it again by hand, and he had it before he left. Then she opened 413. Address: *back for my coat*. She marked it done. At closing, hook 413 was empty for the first time since June. Clodagh didn't see anyone take the coat.
options.senior: Retry what can pass and stop retrying what can't. A cap of 3 tries frees the worker. The dead-letter queue keeps the ticket so a person can fix it and send it again. And the two alarms cover the two ways a queue fails quietly: tickets that can't be sent, and tickets that wait too long. Next, wait longer between tries, with backoff and a little random jitter, so a provider's bad night gets room to recover. Check the address at signup, before the 202. And make sending idempotent, safe to repeat, because a ticket can be handed out twice.

sim.title: Run the box at the Mothlight
sim.lede: You're Fenna, replaying Saturday night at the Mothlight from 22:59:50. From 22:00 a guest signs up every 10 seconds; at 23:00 the late train brings 600 in a minute, 10 a second; the door shuts at 03:00. The web server works on 8 signups at once. Saving one takes 0.1 s, and the email provider takes 1.5 s per email. Before May the server sent the email before it answered, 1.6 s a signup; if the send failed it tried once more, and if that failed too it answered with an error. Since May it saves the signup, drops a ticket in the box and answers 202 at once, and free workers take the ticket on top and send the email. A failed ticket goes back on top, and the worker that failed it is the first one free, so it takes it again at once: the sim never waits between tries, so there's no backoff. Worker-1 starts on June's ticket 413, which has failed 6,854,400 times, once every 1.5 s for 119 days. At 02:00:00 ticket 2035 signs up with a comma where the dot goes. On the provider's bad night, every fifth email fails its first try with a 503 and goes through on the second. p95 and busy cover the last 10 seconds. A ticket's age counts from its guest's signup, and only while it waits in the box. Stuck counts tickets that have failed 3 or more times and are still being tried. Changing a setting replays the night. The clock runs 10 times faster than real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press nothing and watch the late train at 23:00: every guest is answered in 0.1 s, while the box climbs to 559 by 23:01 with only worker-2 sending. The oldest ticket passes 10 minutes at 23:10:42.9, the last guest off the train gets the email at 23:15:00.1, and the box is empty at 23:17:27.1. Switch to Before May: all 8 threads busy at 23:00:00.7, a p95 of 30.4 s at 23:01 and 61.6 s at 23:02:10. Back to Since May, pick 3 tries, then the dead-letter queue: 413 is parked at 22:59:51.5 and the box is empty at 23:08:01.6. Skip to 01:59:50 with each retry rule and watch ticket 2035, then skip to 03:00. Last, try a festival night with one worker, then two, and the provider's bad night.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the arches was haunted but the retry rule, the rule for trying a failed job again. Fenna's box let the web server answer every guest in 0.1 seconds. But a failed ticket went back on top forever, so ticket 413 has held a worker since June, and from 02:00 ticket 2035 held the other. There was no dead-letter queue to park failed tickets, and no alarm on how long the oldest ticket had waited, so nobody saw the box stop.

steps.title: Slow work inside a request holds up the guest and a thread.
steps.text: Before May every signup was synchronous, done while the guest waited. It ran in three steps. First, the server saved the signup, which took 0.1 seconds. Next, it sent the welcome email, which took 1.5; when the provider was slow, this step was slow too. Last, it answered the phone. One thread, one of the server's 8 pairs of hands, was busy for the whole 1.6 seconds. The email was the bottleneck, the slowest step that holds up the rest. So 8 threads finished at most 5 signups a second. The late train brings 10 a second for a minute, so the line grows by 5 a second. By 23:01, 296 guests are waiting for a thread. The p95 response time, the wait 95 of every 100 guests stay within, is 30.4 seconds, and the slowest guest watches a spinner, the turning circle that means wait, for 61.6. Yet the email doesn't change the answer the guest needs, which is "you're on the list". Work like that is the first thing to move out of the request: sending an email, resizing an image, making a PDF (a document file), or calling a slow dependency, another service you rely on.

steps.title: Answer now, do it later: producers, a queue and workers.
steps.text: Since May the request does only what the guest needs, in three steps. First, it saves the signup in the database, the store that keeps the club's records. Next, it puts a job on a queue. Then it answers 202 Accepted with the ticket number. That takes 0.1 seconds, so the whole rush keeps about one thread busy and the line never forms. The web server is the producer, the side that puts jobs in. The workers are consumers, the side that takes them out. Each worker repeats its own steps, side by side with the other. It takes the job at the head, the front of the queue. It sends the email. If the send works, it takes the next job; if it fails, the job goes back. RFC 9110, the official rulebook for HTTP, the web's request language, calls 202 intentionally noncommittal: the work might still not happen. So the answer ought to point to a status monitor, somewhere the guest can check. Here that's the phone screen that says the email is on its way. Keep the queue durable, meaning it is saved so a restart loses no tickets. The cost: the email now arrives later than the answer. And if it never arrives, nobody is at the door to notice.

steps.title: A queue smooths a spike only if the workers drain it.
steps.text: A queue absorbs a burst, a sudden crowd: 600 tickets arrive in a minute and the workers send them at their own pace. The drain rate is how fast the workers empty the queue. The backlog is the work still waiting. While arrivals beat the drain rate, the backlog grows by the difference. Afterwards it shrinks by the difference. Two workers at 1.5 seconds each drain about 1.3 a second. So the rush's last email goes out at 23:07:30.2, 390 seconds after its guest signed up. With worker-1 stuck on 413 it was one worker at about 0.7 a second, and 840 seconds. If arrivals stay above the drain rate, the backlog never drains. On a festival night, a guest a second, one worker sending about 0.7 a second leaves 5,344 tickets waiting at 03:00. Amazon's Builders' Library, a set of articles by Amazon's engineers, calls this bimodal, meaning it has two moods: fine while you keep up, and a long recovery once you fall behind. More workers raise the drain rate. So does making each job cheaper, meaning quicker to do.

steps.title: Retry what can pass, park what can't.
steps.text: A send can fail in two ways. A transient failure passes, like a 503, the too-busy code, from a provider having a bad night. A permanent failure never will, like an address that isn't one. Fenna's rule put every failure back on top. RabbitMQ's docs describe what follows: a requeued message, one put back, goes back at or near the head, and consumers that keep requeueing it make a requeue/redelivery loop. A poison message, one that fails every time, holds a worker forever in that loop: 413 has failed about 6.9 million times. The fix runs in steps. First, the worker tries the job and the try is counted. Second, if it fails below the cap, it waits and tries again. For transient failures, use exponential backoff, a wait that doubles each time, plus jitter, a small random extra. Retrying too fast hammers a provider that is already struggling. Third, once the cap is reached, the job moves to a dead-letter queue, where it waits for a person instead of a worker. A cap set too low parks jobs that would have gone through on the next try. SQS does it with maxReceiveCount, and RabbitMQ's quorum queues with a delivery limit (since 4.3, failed deliveries only). Fourth, an alarm tells someone the DLQ holds something; a DLQ nobody reads helps nobody. Last, that person fixes the cause, then redrives the jobs, sending them back to the main queue. And because queues like SQS deliver at least once, a job can run twice. So make it idempotent, safe to repeat. For example, use the ticket number as an idempotency key, a label that marks the job as done: record each send, and check for it before sending. Season 4 goes deeper.

steps.title: Watch the oldest job's age, not just the count.
steps.text: A queue hides trouble: the door looked fine all night while the box filled. Queue depth says how many jobs are waiting. The age of the oldest says how late the work is, which is what guests feel. 359 waiting at 03:00 could be a busy night, but an oldest ticket of 3,590 seconds is an outage. An age alarm runs in steps. First, SQS sends the oldest ticket's age to CloudWatch, Amazon's service for tracking numbers. Next, CloudWatch compares it with the line you set, here 10 minutes; set the line too high and the alarm rings late. Then, once the age crosses it, the alarm sends someone a message; if nobody owns that alarm, it rings for no one. It would have rung at 23:10:42.9, when ticket 790 had waited 10 minutes. SQS sends the depth to CloudWatch too. Order isn't promised either. A standard SQS queue, the default kind, only tries to keep order and may deliver messages out of order, and any retry reorders jobs. If order matters, use a FIFO queue, short for first in, first out, or make jobs that don't care about order.

diagram.aria: The fix, replayed for Saturday from 22:59:50 to 03:00. Guests' phones send 10 signups a second at 23:00. The web server answers each with 202 and the ticket number in 0.1 seconds and drops a ticket in the box, which holds 519 at 23:01 and is empty by 23:08:01.6. Both workers send, 3 tries per ticket. Tickets that fail 3 tries go to the dead-letter queue, which holds 2, tickets 413 and 2035, with an alarm at the first. The alarm on the oldest ticket's age, at 10 minutes, stays quiet: the oldest never passes 390 seconds.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for Saturday with 3 tries and a dead-letter queue. The web server still answers every signup with a 202 in 0.1 seconds. Ticket 413 is parked at 22:59:51.5 on its 6,854,401st failed try, and the dead-letter queue's alarm rings. Both workers take the late train's tickets: 519 waiting at 23:01, the last email sent at 23:07:30.2 and the box empty at 23:08:01.6. The oldest ticket's age never passes 390 seconds, so the age alarm stays quiet. Ticket 2035 is parked at 02:00:04.6 after 3 tries, and the alarm rings again.

fix.title: The fix: cap the tries, park failures in a dead-letter queue, and alarm on it and on the oldest ticket's age
fix.text: Give each ticket 3 tries. Between tries, wait longer each time with exponential backoff, plus a little random jitter, so a provider's bad night gets room to recover; the sim retries at once and leaves that out. After the third failure, move the ticket to a dead-letter queue instead of back on top, so the worker moves on. Set one alarm for when the dead-letter queue holds anything, and one for when the oldest ticket in the box has waited 10 minutes. Then read what's parked, fix the cause and redrive it, sending it back to the box. Add validation at signup, a check that the address looks like one, before the 202. Then a guest with a comma in the address hears about it at the door. Make sending idempotent, safe to repeat: record each ticket's send and check before sending, because a ticket can be handed out twice. And run enough workers for the rush: with two sending, the late train's last email goes out at 23:07:30.2.

limits: The guest waits longer for the result. The answer is fast, but the email arrives seconds or minutes later, and if it fails the guest has already gone in. Anything the guest needs before the answer, like a check that the address looks real, has to stay in the request. The rest needs a status monitor, a place the guest can check on it.

A queue moves trouble out of sight. Without alarms on the oldest job's age and on the dead-letter queue, a stuck worker or a slow drain shows up only when someone complains. And a backlog has to be paid back: while work arrives faster than the workers empty the queue, it waits, however big the queue.

Order and single delivery aren't promised. A standard SQS queue delivers at least once and only tries to keep order, and every retry reorders jobs. So jobs should be idempotent, safe to repeat, and shouldn't depend on order unless you use a FIFO (first in, first out) queue.

explain.seniorTake: Keep in the request only what the user needs before the answer, and put the rest on a queue. Answer 202 with a way to check, and let workers do the job at their own pace. Then plan for failure from the first day. Jobs will fail, some for a moment and some forever. So cap the tries, wait longer between them, park what still fails in a dead-letter queue, and make jobs idempotent, safe to repeat, because they will sometimes run twice. Run enough workers that, after a spike, they empty the queue faster than new jobs arrive. Watch the oldest job's age as well as the depth, with alarms on it and on the dead-letter queue. A queue nobody watches is a place where work disappears quietly.

realWorld.title: 202 Accepted, in RFC 9110
realWorld.text: RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (June 2022), is the official rulebook for how web requests and answers work. It defines 202 Accepted as a request that has been accepted for processing, but whose processing has not been completed. It says the request might or might not eventually be acted upon. HTTP has no way to send a second status code later, once background work finishes. The RFC calls the response intentionally noncommittal. It lets a server accept a request for some other process, perhaps a batch-oriented one that runs once per day, without the client's connection staying open until it's done. The client is the phone or program that asked. The response ought to describe the request's current status and point to (or embed) a status monitor that can estimate when it will be fulfilled.

realWorld.title: SQS hides a message; it doesn't remove it
realWorld.text: Amazon SQS doesn't remove a message when a consumer receives it. It works in steps. First, a consumer receives the message. Next, SQS hides it from the others for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default and at most 12 hours. Then the consumer does the job and deletes the message. If it isn't deleted before the timeout expires, the message becomes visible again and can be retrieved by another consumer. Because SQS delivers at least once, the docs add, there's no absolute guarantee that a message won't be delivered more than once during the visibility timeout. Among the best practices on the same page: configure a dead-letter queue, so messages that keep failing stop going round and round the main queue.

realWorld.title: SQS dead-letter queues
realWorld.text: In SQS, a source queue, the main one, can name a dead-letter queue for messages that aren't processed successfully. The docs say DLQs are useful for debugging, finding out why something went wrong, because you can isolate unconsumed messages to find out why processing failed. maxReceiveCount is how many times a consumer can receive a message before it moves to the DLQ. Set it as low as 1 and one failure moves it, so the docs advise setting it high enough to allow for sufficient retries. They also note one detail for a standard queue whose maxReceiveCount is greater than 3: a message received 3 or more times without being deleted is moved to the back of the queue. And a DLQ's retention period, how long it keeps a message, should be longer than its source queue's.

realWorld.title: At least once, so make it idempotent
realWorld.text: The SQS docs explain why a message can come back after you delete it. SQS stores copies on several servers. If one of them is unavailable when you delete the message, that server's copy isn't deleted, and it can be delivered again later. Their advice is to design applications to be idempotent, safe to repeat, so they aren't affected adversely when they process the same message more than once.

realWorld.title: Standard queues: best-effort order
realWorld.text: SQS standard queues ensure at-least-once delivery. But because they are spread over many servers, more than one copy of a message might be delivered, and messages may occasionally arrive out of order. They make a best-effort attempt to keep the order the messages were sent in, which means they try but don't promise. The page lists one use: decoupling live user requests from intensive background work, so the user's answer doesn't wait for the heavy job.

realWorld.title: What SQS lets you watch
realWorld.text: SQS sends CloudWatch metrics, numbers tracked over time, for every queue. ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible reflects the current processing backlog, the work waiting. The docs say a value that stays high may point to too few consumers or stuck processing logic. For a dead-letter queue, it's the metric to set an alarm on. ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage is the age of the oldest unprocessed message. One caveat: poison-pill messages, those received again and again but never deleted, are left out of that age metric until they're processed successfully. So it shows the work piling up behind a stuck message rather than the stuck message itself.

realWorld.title: A dead-letter queue still forgets
realWorld.text: SQS keeps a message for 4 days by default, and the retention period can be set from 60 seconds up to 1,209,600 seconds, 14 days. So a dead-letter queue nobody reads still loses what it holds when the retention period runs out, which is one more reason to alarm on it.

realWorld.title: Redrive, after the fix
realWorld.text: Once the cause is fixed, SQS's dead-letter queue redrive moves unconsumed messages from a DLQ to another queue to be processed. By default that's back to the source queue, the one they came from. You can cap the speed, with a custom maximum of up to 500 messages a second, so the workers aren't swamped.

realWorld.title: RabbitMQ: the requeue loop
realWorld.text: RabbitMQ is a message broker, a program that holds queues and hands messages from producers to consumers. Its docs cover consumer acknowledgements, the consumer's word back that a message is done. They say a requeued message is placed at its original position in its queue if possible, or otherwise closer to the head, and may be immediately ready for redelivery. If all consumers requeue because they can't process a delivery for a transient reason, they create a requeue/redelivery loop. That is costly in network bandwidth and CPU, the network's carrying room and the computer's thinking time. Consumers can count the redeliveries and reject messages for good, or requeue after a delay. Any delivery not acknowledged when its connection closes is requeued automatically. So consumers must be prepared for redeliveries and built with idempotence, being safe to repeat, in mind.

realWorld.title: RabbitMQ: poison messages and the delivery limit
realWorld.text: RabbitMQ's quorum queues, a kind that keeps copies on several servers, handle poison messages. Its docs describe these as messages that make a consumer requeue a delivery over and over, so it's never consumed completely and positively acknowledged. Since RabbitMQ 4.0 their delivery limit defaults to 20. A message redelivered more times than that is dropped, or moved to a dead-letter queue if one is set up. The docs recommend a dead letter configuration on every quorum queue so messages aren't dropped and lost by accident. They advise against turning the limit off, because repeated requeues can threaten the stability of the queue and the RabbitMQ servers. Since RabbitMQ 4.3 the limit counts only failed deliveries, such as a consumer crash or a basic.reject, a firm refusal. So a consumer that hands a message back with basic.nack, a softer refusal, can requeue it forever without reaching the limit. Count the tries in the consumer too.

realWorld.title: Amazon: alarm on the age
realWorld.text: The Amazon Builders' Library article Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs says a queue increases a system's durability and availability: work is less likely to be lost, and the service keeps answering. The price is occasional increased latency, extra waiting, due to retries. When processing stops but messages keep arriving, a large backlog can make work complete too late to be useful. It warns that even short load spikes can mean multi-hour recovery times. The team alarms if there are any messages in a dead-letter queue, because that means a bug to fix, and the DLQ lets it re-process the messages after the fix. But DLQ information arrives too late to rely on alone. And the latency producers see only mirrors the queue service's own, not the workers'. So the team focuses more on measuring the age of messages in the queue. That quickly catches systems that are behind, or erroring out and retrying.

asked: When would you use a queue instead of doing the work in the request?
What happens if the consumer is slower than the producer?
What is a dead-letter queue for?
interview.answer: Use a queue when the work doesn't change the answer the user needs right now, and it is slow or depends on something slow or unreliable. Examples are sending email, resizing images, making PDFs and calling a third party, another company's service. The request saves what it must, puts a job on a durable queue, one that survives a restart, and answers at once. Often that's 202 Accepted with a way to check the status. Workers do the job at their own pace, and a spike waits in the queue instead of holding threads. If consumers are slower than producers, the backlog grows by the difference for as long as that lasts. A short spike is fine if the workers empty the queue afterwards. A steady shortfall grows without limit, and the age of the oldest message grows with it. Add consumers or make each job cheaper. If you still can't keep up, slow the producers down or turn some work away. Either way, alarm on the oldest message's age, not only the depth. A dead-letter queue is where a message goes after failing a set number of times, maxReceiveCount in SQS. So a poison message stops holding a worker and isn't lost: alarm on it, read it, fix the cause and redrive it. Then mention the details. Retry transient failures, the ones that pass, with backoff and jitter, and cap the tries. And make jobs idempotent, safe to repeat, because most queues deliver at least once.

terms.def: Done while the caller waits: the answer comes only after the work is finished. Before May, the Mothlight's server sent each welcome email inside the signup request.
Done after the answer, so the caller doesn't wait for it. Also called background work.
A waiting line of jobs that workers do after the user has had their answer, so slow work doesn't hold up the user or one of the server's threads.
One piece of work put on a queue to be done later, like sending one welcome email.
A program that puts jobs on a queue. At the Mothlight it's the web server.
A program that takes jobs off a queue and does them. Also called a worker.
A consumer: a program that takes the next job from a queue, does it, then takes the next. The Mothlight has two, sending welcome emails.
One item on a queue, such as a job. SQS and RabbitMQ call them messages.
A server that holds queues and hands messages from producers to consumers, such as RabbitMQ.
Fenna's word for a job in the box: one guest's welcome email, numbered. The number is also the guest's hook in the cloakroom.
Fenna's name for the Mothlight's queue of tickets. A free worker takes the ticket on top; in her version, a failed one goes back on top.
One guest's form, a name and an email address, sent to the club's web server to put them on the list.
The email a guest gets after signing up, with the code that lets them back in after a smoke.
A service that sends email for you. Your app hands it each message, and it answers whether the send was accepted.
The status code, the number at the start of an answer, that means: I have your request, and it isn't finished. The answer should say where to check on it, like a cloakroom ticket.
Somewhere a user can check how their request is going and roughly when it will be done. At the Mothlight, the phone screen saying the email is on its way. The name comes from RFC 9110.
Work waiting to be done, here the tickets in the box. It grows while jobs arrive faster than workers finish them, and shrinks when they arrive slower.
How many messages are waiting in a queue right now.
How long the message at the front of a queue has waited. It shows a stuck or slow queue even when the depth looks normal.
How fast workers take jobs off a queue: the number of workers divided by the time a job takes. Two workers at 1.5 s each drain about 1.3 a second.
The front: the next message to be handed out. Fenna calls it the top of the box.
To put a message that couldn't be handled back on the queue, so it can be delivered again.
Handing a message to a consumer again after it was requeued or never acknowledged.
RabbitMQ's name for workers taking a message, failing, putting it back and taking it again, over and over. It uses up the network and the computer's time and gets nothing done.
A message that fails every time it's tried, like an email address with a comma in it, so retrying can never work. Also called a poison pill.
A failure that may pass if you try again later, like a 503 from a busy provider.
A failure that will happen every time, like an address that isn't an email address. Retrying it wastes the worker.
A separate queue where messages go after failing a set number of times, so they stop holding up the main queue and a person can look, fix the cause and send them again.
A post office department that opened letters it could neither deliver nor return, to find out where they belonged.
The setting in an SQS redrive policy: how many times a message can be received before it's moved to the dead-letter queue.
The SQS settings on a queue that name its dead-letter queue and its maxReceiveCount.
Moving messages from a dead-letter queue back to a queue for processing, usually after fixing what made them fail.

In a RabbitMQ quorum queue, how many times a message may be handed out again before it's dropped or sent to a dead-letter queue. 20 by default since 4.0; since 4.3, messages handed back with nack don't count.

Two ways a RabbitMQ consumer can refuse a message, putting it back on the queue if it asks to. Since 4.3 a reject counts toward a quorum queue's delivery limit and a nack, short for basic.nack, doesn't.
A RabbitMQ queue type that keeps copies on several servers and counts how many times each message has been delivered.
How long SQS hides a message after a consumer receives it. If it isn't deleted by then, it becomes visible again and another consumer can get it. 30 seconds by default.
Telling the queue a message is done so it's removed. In SQS a consumer deletes a message after handling it; until then it's only hidden.
A promise that every message is delivered, sometimes more than once. The consumer has to cope with copies.
SQS's default kind of queue. Every message arrives at least once, sometimes twice, and SQS tries to keep the order but doesn't promise it.
First in, first out: an SQS queue type that keeps messages in the order they were sent.
How long a queue keeps a message before deleting it. SQS keeps one 4 days by default, and up to 14.
Simple Queue Service: a queue that Amazon Web Services runs for you, so you rent it instead of running your own.
A widely used message broker that teams often run on their own servers.
A file format for documents that look the same on every screen and printer, like a receipt or a ticket.
A number SQS reports to CloudWatch, Amazon's tracking service: how long the oldest message still waiting in a queue has waited.
A number SQS reports to CloudWatch, Amazon's tracking service: how many messages are waiting to be handed out. That is the backlog.
A rule in CloudWatch that watches one tracked number and messages someone when it crosses a line you set, like a queue's oldest message passing 10 minutes. A smoke alarm for a system.
Checking input when it arrives, such as whether an email address looks like one, so bad data is turned away while the user is still there to fix it.
A time when a system isn't doing its job for its users, even if parts of it still answer.
Finding out why a program went wrong.
Amazon's collection of articles by its engineers on how Amazon builds and runs services.
Having two modes. A queue-based system is quick while it keeps up and very slow once a backlog builds, with little in between.

atWork: Think of a signup flow that sends its welcome email inside the request: when the email provider slows down, signups time out, giving up after too long a wait. Find one like it in a system you can read: any request that waits on an email, a PDF, an image or a call to another company's service. Read-only access is enough. How long does that step take at p95, the wait 95 of every 100 requests stay within? And how many threads does the server have? If the work is already on a queue, open the queue's settings. Is there a redrive policy, the settings that name a dead-letter queue, and what's maxReceiveCount, the number of tries? In CloudWatch, Amazon's tracking service, chart ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage and ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible for the queue and its dead-letter queue over the last busy day. Is there an alarm on the oldest message's age, and one on any message in the dead-letter queue? Do the workers wait longer between tries, and is sending idempotent, safe to repeat? If not, draft the fix: answer 202 and put the job on a queue; workers with capped retries, backoff and jitter; a dead-letter queue; and alarms on the queue's age and on the dead-letter queue.

recall.prompt: Your shop's checkout makes a PDF receipt, a document file, before it answers. A PDF takes 3 seconds, the server handles 20 checkouts at once, and on sale days checkouts give up waiting. What would you change, and what new things do you have to watch afterwards?

keyIdeas.idea: Move the PDF out of the request: save the order, put a job on a queue, answer at once, and let workers make the PDF
Each checkout holds a thread for the whole 3 seconds, so 20 at once is under 7 checkouts a second
Jobs can fail and can run twice: capped retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue, and idempotent jobs
Watch the queue's depth and its oldest job's age, and give the customer a way to check on the receipt

recall.model: Making the PDF doesn't change whether the order went through, so it doesn't belong in the request. Each checkout holds a thread for 3 seconds, so 20 at once is under 7 checkouts a second, and on a sale day the rest wait until they time out. Instead, take three steps: save the order, put a make-the-receipt job on a queue, and answer at once, with the order page or 202 and a link to check. Workers make the PDF and email it. Then plan for failure: retry with backoff, waiting longer each time, and a cap. Send what keeps failing to a dead-letter queue with an alarm. And make the job idempotent, safe to repeat, because it may run twice. Watch the queue's depth and the age of its oldest job, and run enough workers to empty a sale-day backlog.

recall.prompt: Signups arrive at 10 a second for one minute. Two workers each send one email every 1.5 seconds, and nothing else is waiting. About how many tickets are waiting when the minute ends?
recall.why: Two workers send about 1.3 a second, so in 60 seconds they send about 80 of the 600. The Mothlight's sim, with 413 parked, has 519 waiting at 23:01. The backlog grows by arrivals minus the drain rate, how fast the workers empty the queue. Afterwards it shrinks by the drain rate minus arrivals.

recall.prompt: Orders arrive at 50 a second all day. Your three workers can process 40 a second between them. What happens to the queue over the day, and what do you do about it?

keyIdeas.idea: The backlog grows by 10 a second without end: 36,000 an hour, and each order waits longer than the last
Raise the drain rate: more workers, or cheaper jobs
Alarm on the age of the oldest message, not only the depth
If you still can't keep up, slow the producers or turn work away instead of letting the queue grow

recall.model: The queue gains 10 orders a second, 36,000 an hour, and never drains. Every order waits longer than the one before, so the age of the oldest message climbs all day. A queue only smooths a spike if the workers empty it faster than orders arrive afterwards. Add a fourth worker or more, or make each order cheaper, quicker to process, so the drain rate tops 50 a second with room to spare. Alarm on the oldest message's age as well as the depth. If you still can't keep up, slow the producers down or turn some work away, instead of letting the backlog grow without bound.

recall.prompt: What is a dead-letter queue for?
options: Messages that arrive out of order, held back until the gap is filled
Spare room for messages when the main queue is full, so none are lost
Messages older than the queue's retention period, kept a little longer
Messages that failed too many times, kept for a person to fix and resend
recall.why: After maxReceiveCount tries in SQS, or the delivery limit in RabbitMQ, a failing message moves to the dead-letter queue. So it stops holding a worker and isn't lost. Alarm on it, read it, fix the cause and send it back. A dead-letter queue isn't a fix by itself: it's a place to look.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Fenna moved the box to Amazon SQS, the queue Amazon runs for you. A ticket goes to the dead-letter queue after it has been handed out 3 times, and there are alarms on that queue and on the oldest ticket's age. In February the email provider slowed down, and a send started taking about 40 seconds. SQS gives a worker 30 seconds with a ticket before the others can see it again. That Saturday guests got two and three copies of the same welcome email. And by 23:30 the dead-letter queue was filling with tickets whose emails had all gone out.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did guests get the same email two and three times, why did sent tickets end up in the dead-letter queue, and what should Fenna change?

keyIdeas.idea: The send took longer than the visibility timeout, so the ticket became visible again and another worker sent it too
Each of those receives counted toward maxReceiveCount, so tickets that had really been sent reached the limit and went to the DLQ
Raise the visibility timeout above the slowest send, or extend it while a send runs, and put a timeout on the provider call
Make sending idempotent: record each ticket's send and check before sending

coldCase.model: SQS doesn't remove a ticket when a worker takes it. It hides it for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds here, and the worker deletes it when it's done. With sends taking 40 seconds, it went like this. A worker took a ticket and started sending. At 30 seconds the ticket became visible again, in the middle of its send. Another worker took it and sent it again: two or three copies. Each of those receives counted toward maxReceiveCount, so tickets that had really been sent reached 3 and were moved to the dead-letter queue. Raise the visibility timeout above the slowest send you expect, or extend it while a send is still running. And put a timeout on the provider call, a limit on how long to wait, so a send can't run forever. Make sending idempotent, safe to repeat: record each ticket's send and check it first, so a redelivered ticket sends nothing. Then redrive the parked tickets, sending them back to the box: the check skips the ones already sent.
